title: Code World Model: Building World Models for Computation – Jacob Kahn, FAIR Meta

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary object is a 32B parameter dense transformer modeling program execution dynamics, scaling laws, and intrinsic reasoning capabilities, fitting Model Foundations & Behavior. CWM is a code reasoning model targeting software-engineering tasks like execution tracing and neural debugging, aligning with Coding Assistants. The talk covers pre-training on trillions of tokens, post-training with SFT and asynchronous RL, and evaluation of execution-trace accuracy. Prerequisites include autoregressive models, reinforcement learning, and computability theory, indicating an advanced audience. The talk presents a research model with a detailed technical report, fitting a research talk format. Multiple high-grade transcript anchors directly support each classification dimension with specific quantitative and qualitative claims.

summary: Jacob Kahn introduces the Code World Model (CWM), a research effort at FAIR Meta aimed at building models that reason, plan, and make decisions, using code as a constrained sandbox. The core thesis is that standard token-based autoregressive models only see syntax, whereas true program reasoning requires modeling execution dynamics. CWM addresses this by implicitly predicting the transition function of program states, representing execution as line-by-line traces with local variables and frame separators that map directly to source lines. These execution traces function like chain-of-thought reasoning that an LLM can generate autogressively, enabling imagined simulation before real execution. Kahn argues the dichotomy between world models and LLMs is false: world models parameterize a problem and LLMs use that parameterization. CWM is a 32-billion parameter dense transformer with long context, trained end-to-end including pre-training on trillions of tokens, domain-specific mid-training, instruction fine-tuning, and joint RL with agentic reasoning. The training data leverages large-scale GitHub PRs with mutation, test execution, and repo-level execution trace generation. The post-training infrastructure uses a highly asynchronous RL pipeline with queued model checkpoints and trajectories, enabling mid-trajectory model updates with strong on-policy guarantees despite slight off-policy drift. CWM is deliberately bash-oriented with fewer tools, forcing it to learn terminal usage end-to-end similar to a real engineer. Rejection sampling on failed agentic traces feeds back into SFT before RL. Kahn reports CWM traces code execution line by line with very high accuracy, showing local variable values at specific points with precision. This enables capabilities like a neural debugger where users express program shape and semantics inline with code, letting the model fill in gaps by simulating execution. Kahn also envisions ambitious applications: approximating undecidable problems like the halting problem through simulated execution, and debugging expensive distributed systems without real execution. The model and code are available on Hugging Face and GitHub, with a technical report detailing training and data.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.summary: Kahn introduces CWM as a world model for computation, aiming to build models that reason, plan, and make decisions using code as a sandbox. He frames world models as a parameterization of a problem and LLMs as a way to use that parameterization, arguing the dichotomy between them is false.

sections.title: Modeling Execution vs Syntax
sections.summary: Kahn contrasts standard token-based code modeling (syntax only) with CWM's approach of modeling execution explicitly via line-by-line traces with local variables and frame separators. He explains execution traces can extend to repo-level and systems-level scope, and that both program execution and agent decisions can be modeled as transition functions.

sections.title: World Models for Agentic Reasoning
sections.summary: Kahn describes how world models enable imagined simulation before real execution, allowing agents to get feedback in an imagined environment. Execution traces become chain-of-thought that an LLM can autogressively generate, predicting state-action-to-state transitions.

sections.title: Data and Training Pipeline
sections.summary: CWM data collection uses large-scale GitHub PRs with mutation, test/CI execution, and repo-level execution trace generation. The model is a 32-billion parameter dense transformer trained end-to-end: pre-training on trillions of tokens, domain-specific mid-training, long-context mid-training, instruction fine-tuning, and joint RL with agentic reasoning.

sections.title: Bash-Oriented Agentic Setup and SFT
sections.summary: CWM uses fewer tools with heavy emphasis on bash, learning terminal commands end-to-end similar to a real engineer. SFT before RL uses rejection sampling on failed agentic traces, such as searching for instantiation logic via grep.

sections.title: Asynchronous RL Infrastructure
sections.summary: Kahn details the asynchronous RL pipeline with samplers, environment execution, trajectory scoring, and gradient computation. Queues for model checkpoints and trajectories keep the system on-policy despite high asynchronicity. Mid-trajectory model updates are possible with strong guarantees due to throughput and data volume. Post-training processed about 200 billion tokens, producing a versatile model that traces code execution with high accuracy.

sections.title: Applications: Neural Debugger and Ambitious CS Problems
sections.summary: Kahn describes how CWM's precise variable tracking enables a neural debugger where users express program shape and semantics inline with code, letting the model fill gaps by simulating execution. He envisions approximating undecidable problems like the halting problem through simulated execution, and debugging expensive distributed systems without real execution. He closes by encouraging the audience to build on CWM, noting availability on Hugging Face, GitHub, and a detailed technical report.
